claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings protect zirconium-alloy cladding under individual service regimes.
Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion causes premature failure of elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding.
Introducing nitrogen during Cr deposition can form a CrN interlayer or discrete CrN barrier regions at the Cr/Zr-alloy interface.
The proposed intervention will produce a dense, finely grained CrN interlayer.
A CrN interlayer reduces atomic mobility between the Cr coating and Zr substrate.
The CrN interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier to Cr and Zr transport at elevated temperatures.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion preserves coating integrity.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion preserves protective oxide formation on the coating's outer surface.
The nitrogen-modified coating will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than an unmodified Cr coating during high-temperature steam exposure.
Reduced interdiffusion will improve coating integrity and longevity relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
The nitrogen-modified coating will maintain oxidation protection comparable to that of unmodified Cr under approximately 300°C subcritical-water exposure.
The proposed benefits are expected during approximately 1200°C short-duration steam exposure.
The proposed benefits are expected during approximately 300°C prolonged subcritical-water exposure.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires oxidation protection under normal conditions to remain comparable to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule requires oxidation behavior and mechanical integrity under both conditions to be measurably improved. A result that is comparable, as predicted, could therefore trigger falsification.
